tasks.title: Shadowing: changing the type under the same name
tasks.statement: Write fn double_text(input: &str) -> i32: trim the whitespace at both ends (trim), parse the number (parse) and return it multiplied by 2. Use shadowing: three times let input = ... with one name, the type changes from &str to i32. The input is always valid (you can unwrap).
tasks.hint: let input: i32 = input.parse().unwrap(); — on the right is still the old &str, on the left already the new i32.

tasks.title: Overflow: four ways
tasks.statement: Write fn add_modes(a: u8, b: u8) -> (u8, Option<u8>, u8, (u8, bool)): the result of addition under four rules — wrapping, checked (None on overflow), saturating and overflowing (the value and a flag). Python knows nothing about overflow, but the processor does.
tasks.hint: Integers have the methods wrapping_add, checked_add, saturating_add, overflowing_add.

tasks.title: The as cast: chopping off bits
tasks.statement: Write fn casts(x: i32) -> (u8, i8, u16, f64): the value x cast with as to u8, i8 and u16, and x as f64 divided by 2. See how as chops off the high bits (two's complement from the chapter on numbers) — there are no exceptions.
tasks.hint: x as u8 takes the low 8 bits; x as i8 interprets them as a signed number.

tasks.title: Counting ones by hand
tasks.statement: Write fn popcount(mut n: u32) -> u32 — the number of one bits — with a loop using a shift and a mask (n & 1, n >> 1). You may not use the count_ones method: the checker looks for it in your code.
tasks.hint: while n != 0 { count += n & 1; n >>= 1; } — a right shift drops the lowest bit.

tasks.title: Division like in Python
tasks.statement: Write fn py_divmod(a: i32, b: i32) -> (i32, i32): integer division and remainder by Python rules (a // b, a % b): the quotient is rounded down, the remainder has the sign of the divisor. By default Rust rounds toward zero, and the remainder takes the sign of the dividend.
tasks.hint: If the remainder is nonzero and its sign differs from the sign of b, decrease the quotient by 1 and add b to the remainder.

tasks.title: Comparing floats with a tolerance
tasks.statement: Write fn approx_eq(a: f64, b: f64) -> bool: the numbers are equal if |a − b| is at most 1e-9 · max(1, |a|, |b|). The exact comparison 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false in any language — recall the chapter on numbers.
tasks.hint: f64 has the methods abs() and max(): (a - b).abs() <= 1e-9 * scale.

tasks.title: A tuple as a result
tasks.statement: Write fn min_max(a: i32, b: i32, c: i32) -> (i32, i32): the smallest and the largest of three. The result is taken apart: let (lo, hi) = min_max(...).
tasks.hint: The methods min and max can be chained: a.min(b).min(c).

tasks.title: An array on the stack: a copy, not a reference
tasks.statement: Write fn reversed(a: [i32; 5]) -> [i32; 5] — a new array in reverse order (indexes and a for loop). An array of known size is copied whole: walk over the cells and make sure the original did not change.
tasks.hint: let mut out = [0; 5]; — an array of five zeros; out[4 - i] = a[i].

tasks.title: Byte order in a number
tasks.statement: Write fn byte_orders(n: u32) -> (String, String): the bytes of the number n in little-endian and big-endian order, in hex separated by spaces. Use the methods u32::to_le_bytes and to_be_bytes.
tasks.hint: to_le_bytes() returns [u8; 4] — an array on the stack; walk over it with the .iter() iterator.

tasks.title: Two's complement by hand
tasks.statement: Write fn to_bits(n: i8) -> String (the 8 binary digits of two's complement: cast n as u8 and print it with {:08b}) and fn from_bits(bits: &str) -> i8 (parse the string with u8::from_str_radix(bits, 2) and cast as i8).
tasks.hint: as between integers of the same width computes nothing — it changes the interpretation of the same eight bits.

tasks.title: Type sizes in memory
tasks.statement: Write fn sizes() -> Vec<(&'static str, usize)>: pairs (type name, std::mem::size_of) for: u8, i32, u64, char, bool, (u8, u32), [u16; 5], &str, usize — in exactly this order. Note the alignment of the tuple and that &str is two words (a pointer and a length).
tasks.hint: size_of::<T>() is a compile-time function. The tuple (u8, u32) takes 8 bytes: u32 is aligned to four.

tasks.title: Which way the stack grows
tasks.statement: The driver calls nested functions and writes the addresses of their local variables into the slice addrs (from the outer call to the inner one). Write fn grows_down(addrs: &[usize]) -> bool: true if each next address is strictly smaller than the previous one (the stack grows toward smaller addresses, as in the chapter on the processor).
tasks.hint: A &[usize] slice is a view of an array of numbers: iterate over the indexes 1..addrs.len().

tasks.title: Deep recursion vs the stack
tasks.statement: The recursive sum_to(n) builds a frame for every step and overflows the stack for n = 20 million (in Python this would be a RecursionError at a thousand). Rewrite sum_to as a loop with the same result.
tasks.hint: Each recursive call is a new frame on the stack; a loop uses a single frame.

tasks.title: Leap year and days in a month
tasks.statement: Write fn is_leap(year: u32) -> bool and fn days_in_month(year: u32, month: u32) -> u32 (a match on the month number; in February take leap years into account). For a month outside 1..=12 call panic!("bad month") — a panic is like ValueError in Python, but it cannot be caught.
tasks.hint: The pattern 1 | 3 | 5 combines several values in one match arm.

tasks.title: GCD, LCM and overflow protection
tasks.statement: Write fn gcd(a: u64, b: u64) -> u64 (the Euclidean algorithm in a loop) and fn lcm(a: u64, b: u64) -> Option<u64>: the least common multiple, or None if the result does not fit into u64 (use checked_mul).
tasks.hint: lcm = a / gcd * b; check the multiplication with checked_mul — it returns None on overflow.

tasks.title: A number in any numeral system
tasks.statement: Write fn to_base(mut n: u32, base: u32) -> String: the representation of n in a system with base 2..=36, digits 0-9 and a-z. For 0 return "0". Python has format(n, 'b') and int(s, base); here you write it yourself (char::from_digit).
tasks.hint: The remainders come out from the lowest digit to the highest — collect them into a Vec and reverse it with rev().

tasks.title: Sizes instead of getsizeof
tasks.statement:
In Python sys.getsizeof(5) returns 28. Using size_of, print the sizes in bytes for i8, i16, i32, i64, i128, f32, f64, bool, char, (u8, u32), [i32; 10] — on one line separated by spaces: «1 2 4 8 16 4 8 1 4 8 40».

Expected output:
1 2 4 8 16 4 8 1 4 8 40
tasks.hint: use std::mem::size_of; size_of::<T>().

tasks.title: Four results of division
tasks.statement:
For a = -7 and b = 2 print four lines: a / b, a % b, a.div_euclid(b), a.rem_euclid(b). Expected: «-3», «-1», «-4», «1» (in Python: -7 // 2 = -4 and -7 % 2 = 1).

Expected output:
-3
-1
-4
1
tasks.hint: div_euclid and rem_euclid match Python's // and % when the divisor is positive.

tasks.title: Factorial of 30 without bigint
tasks.statement:
In Python 30! is computed without any trouble. In Rust it fits into u128. Compute 30! with a loop and print «265252859812191058636308480000000».

Expected output:
265252859812191058636308480000000
tasks.hint: The u128 type: let mut f: u128 = 1;

tasks.title: Factorial with overflow checking
tasks.statement: Write the function fact(n: u32) -> Option<u64>: n!, or None if the result does not fit into u64 (use checked_mul).
tasks.hint: checked_mul returns an Option; the ? operator returns None from the function.

tasks.title: Rounding like in Python
tasks.statement: Write the function py_round(x: f64) -> i64: rounding to the nearest integer, with halves going to the even number (like round in Python: 0.5 → 0, 1.5 → 2, 2.5 → 2, −0.5 → 0, −1.5 → −2).
tasks.hint: x.round() rounds halves away from zero; if the result is odd and x is exactly a half, step back by one toward zero.

tasks.title: Negative indexes
tasks.statement: Write the function py_get(v: &[i32], i: i32) -> Option<i32>: like v[i] in Python — a negative index counts from the end, going out of bounds gives None.
tasks.hint: Cast len to i32, add it to the negative index and check the bounds.

tasks.title: to_bytes by hand
tasks.statement: Write the functions to_le(n: u32) -> [u8; 4] and from_le(b: [u8; 4]) -> u32 without to_le_bytes — using the shifts >> and << and the mask 0xFF.
tasks.hint: The lowest byte is n & 0xFF; the next one is (n >> 8) & 0xFF.

tasks.title: Struct size
tasks.statement:
Declare two structs with the attribute #[repr(C)]: A { a: u8, b: u32, c: u8 } and B { b: u32, a: u8, c: u8 }. Print size_of::<A>() and size_of::<B>(): «12» and «8» — because of the padding between fields.

Expected output:
12
8
tasks.hint: #[repr(C)] fixes the field order; the order affects the size.

tasks.title: Copying a string
tasks.statement:
Create a = String::from("rust"), a clone b = a.clone(), append the string "!" to b and print both: «rust» and «rust!». In Python you would have to call copy for this.

Expected output (each line is shown in «», the quotes themselves are not printed):
«rust»
«rust!»
tasks.hint: clone() makes a full copy, so a stays intact.

tasks.title: bool is not a number
tasks.statement:
In Python sum([True, False, True]) = 2. In Rust you cannot add bools. Count the number of true values in the vector [true, false, true, true, false] in two ways: with a filter (iter().filter(|b| **b).count()) and with a cast (b as i32). Print two lines «3» and «3».

Expected output:
3
3
tasks.hint: true as i32 == 1; *x dereferences a reference.

tasks.title: Average without mixing types
tasks.statement:
In Python sum(v) / len(v) just works. For v = [3, 4, 4, 6] of i32, print the average as a float with two decimals: «4.25».

Expected output:
4.25
tasks.hint: Cast both the sum and the length to f64.
